definitions.definition: Difference-and-non-difference: Brahman is at once one with and different from souls and world (one as cause, many as effect).
Natural difference-and-non-difference of cit and acit from Brahman, like snake and coils.
Held to be inconceivable (acintya) in the relation of the Lord and his powers.
Bhāskara's form: difference of soul from Brahman is due to real limiting adjuncts (upādhi); non-difference is natural.
Yādavaprakāśa's form (as reported by Rāmānuja): Brahman by nature becomes Īśvara, souls and matter; difference and non-difference are both natural.
Name of Nimbārka's doctrine: the relation of Brahman to souls and world is naturally both difference and non-difference, not due to adjuncts.
'Dual-non-dual': name of Nimbārka's Vedānta, synonymous with svābhāvika-bhedābheda.
A limiting adjunct — body, senses, intellect — that really delimits Brahman as the individual soul; real, not imagined, and removed only at liberation after death.

literal: that which is placed near; limiting condition
notes: Advaita also uses upādhi but holds the adjuncts to be products of avidyā (not ultimately real); Bhāskara insists they are real — same word, different status.

definitions.definition: The doctrine that the world is a real transformation of Brahman (through its śakti).
The world is a real transformation of the Lord's power.
Accepted in the form avikṛta-pariṇāma: transformation without change in Brahman.
Accepted as śakti-pariṇāma: the external power transforms, the Lord remains unchanged.
Unmodified transformation: Brahman becomes the world without any change in itself, as gold in ornaments.
Transformation of the Lord's power (not of the Lord): the world is a real modification of māyā-śakti while the Lord, like a touchstone yielding gold, is unchanged.
The combination of knowledge (meditation on Brahman) with the Vedic and social duties of one's station, maintained until death, as the means to liberation.
The soul as a part of Brahman made distinct by adjuncts.
The soul as a naturally distinct part (power) of the Lord.
The soul as a spark-like part of Brahman in which bliss is concealed.
The soul as a separated part (vibhinnāṃśa), distinct from the Lord's own expansions (svāṃśa).
The soul is atomic in size, dwelling in the heart and pervading the body by its quality of knowledge.
The soul is atomic, a spark of Brahman.
The soul is an infinitesimal particle of consciousness (cit-kaṇa).
Vijñānabhikṣu: non-separation — souls and prakṛti are not separate from Brahman, their substrate, though distinct; his preferred name for the relation.
The released soul's non-separation from Brahman (BS 4.4.4).
The conscious reality: the souls, one of the three realities.
The non-conscious reality, of three kinds: aprākṛta, prākṛta and time.
Non-material 'matter': the substance of the Lord's form and abode, beyond prakṛti.
Transcendental, not of māyā: the Lord's body, name and abode and the devotee's perfected body.
The three realities: cit, acit and Īśvara, established by scripture (Daśaślokī 7).
The five things to be known: the worshipped (upāsya), the worshipper (upāsaka), the fruit of grace, the rasa of devotion, and the obstacles.

notes: The Śrīvaiṣṇava tradition has its own arthapañcaka (Piḷḷai Lokācārya); definitions differ.

definitions.definition: Surrender to the Lord, one of the five means; the refuge of Kṛṣṇa's feet (Daśaślokī 8).
Surrender (śaraṇāgati) with six limbs, underlying all devotion.
Approaching and surrendering to the guru as the means, for one unable to follow the other means.
The divine couple Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa, worshipped together (yugala-upāsanā).
Rādhā–Kṛṣṇa as the object of service in mañjarī-bhāva.
The mood of Rādhā's female companions, in which the devotee witnesses and serves the couple's eternal play (Harivyāsa's Mahāvāṇī).
The companions' mood; the mañjarī-bhāva is a special form of it centred on service to Rādhā.

literal: the mood of a female friend

definitions.definition: Pure non-dualism: Brahman untouched by māyā is the only reality, and the world is its real form.
Grace, the Lord's nourishment (poṣaṇa) of the soul (BhP 2.10.4); the path in which grace alone, independent of means, gives loving service.
The path of rule: devotion and liberation pursued through scriptural discipline and means.
The 'stream': souls carried along in worldly pursuits, outside both grace and rule.
The Lord's grace, identical with puṣṭi.
'Relation with Brahman': the initiation in which the disciple dedicates body, senses, mind, family and wealth to Kṛṣṇa, removing the five kinds of faults (Siddhāntarahasya).
Loving service of the Lord's form: with body (tanujā), wealth (vittajā) and mind (mānasī); the mind flowing to him is sevā itself.
Service in the practitioner's body and in the inner perfected body.
Mental service, the highest form, to which bodily and material service lead.
Absorption in the Lord through forgetting the world, brought about by his play (the theme of the tenth canto).

notes: Homonym: Yoga Sūtra 1.2 uses nirodha for the stilling of mind-activities; Vallabha's nirodha is absorption of attachment in Kṛṣṇa — no equivalence asserted.

definitions.definition: Consuming absorption or 'addiction' to Kṛṣṇa, the culmination of the growth of devotion.
Affection/love, the first growth from the seed of devotion, destroying other attachments.
The stage of love above prema in which the heart melts completely.
Attachment to the Lord that makes household life distasteful (Bhaktivardhinī).
The seventh stage: attachment to the Lord's name, qualities and abode.
Offering: everything is used only after being offered to the Lord; the unoffered is to be avoided.
The imperishable Brahman, Puruṣottama's abode and 'feet', the goal of knowers; lower than Puruṣottama.
The highest person, Kṛṣṇa, above Akṣara Brahman; the goal of grace-devotion.
The world as Brahman's real, divine form, to be honoured, as opposed to saṃsāra.
The soul's own construction of 'I and mine' through ignorance; unreal and to be destroyed — distinct from the world (jagat), which is real.

Manifestation and concealment: Brahman's being, consciousness and bliss are manifest or concealed in its forms; creation and dissolution are manifestation and concealment, not origination and destruction.
Brahman as the locus of contradictory attributes, all true of it.
A body fit for the Lord's service, one of the three fruits of service.
Supernatural capacity to relish the Lord's bliss, the highest fruit of service.
The 'eight seals': the eight poet-singers of the Puṣṭimārga appointed by Viṭṭhalanātha — Sūrdās, Kumbhandās, Paramānanddās, Kṛṣṇadās, Nanddās, Caturbhujdās, Govindsvāmī, Chītsvāmī.
The mansion-temple in which the Lord's form is served as a householder's child and lord, with its own music (havelī saṅgīt).
'Mistress': Rādhā (and the gopīs) as Kṛṣṇa's beloved, emphasised by Viṭṭhalanātha.
Qualified non-dualism of Śiva: Śiva with cit-śakti is one, with souls and world as his body.
Śiva's power of consciousness, inseparable from him, identified with Umā and with the supreme ether; the world subsists in it subtly.
The small space in the lotus of the heart (Chāndogya 8.1), identified with Śiva as the supreme ether and the seat of meditation.
The supreme ether: Śiva's cit-śakti, the ākāśa of the Upaniṣads read as Brahman.
Equality with Śiva: the released soul shares his bliss and powers except world-governance.
Śrīpati's doctrine: non-duality of Śiva and soul, both qualified by Śakti (in Śiva as power, in the soul as devotion), realised as their union.
The union in equal essence of the liṅga (Śiva) and the aṅga (soul), the goal of Śakti-viśiṣṭādvaita (Śrīkarabhāṣya).

literal: equal flavour of liṅga and aṅga

definitions.definition: Inconceivable simultaneous difference and non-difference of the Lord and his powers (souls, world); inconceivable because his powers are beyond reason.
Inconceivable: what cannot be established or refuted by reasoning and is known only from revelation — used of the Lord's powers.
The Lord's internal, essential power, of three aspects (sandhinī, saṃvit, hlādinī), which constitutes his form, abode and associates.
The marginal power: the souls, 'on the border' between the internal and external powers, able to turn to either.
The external power, māyā, which produces the material world and covers the souls turned away from the Lord.
The pleasure-giving aspect of the internal power; its essence is prema and its fullest embodiment is Rādhā.
The existence aspect of the internal power, manifesting the Lord's abode, form and paraphernalia.
The knowledge aspect of the internal power, by which the Lord knows and makes himself known.
The Lord himself — Kṛṣṇa — of whom all other forms are portions (BhP 1.3.28, the governing statement).
The relish of love for Kṛṣṇa, when the permanent emotion of love combines with its excitants, effects, bodily signs and transient emotions; the highest rasa.
The permanent emotion underlying a rasa; in bhakti-rasa, love for Kṛṣṇa (kṛṣṇa-rati) in one of five primary or seven secondary forms.
The excitants of rasa: the object and substratum (ālambana: Kṛṣṇa and his devotees) and the stimuli (uddīpana: his qualities, flute, dress, places).

literal: that which causes to be felt

definitions.definition: The outward expressions of emotion: dancing, rolling, singing, crying out, and the like.
The eight involuntary bodily signs of ecstasy: stupor, sweating, horripilation, faltering voice, trembling, change of colour, tears, fainting.
The thirty-three transient emotions that move within the permanent emotion.
Love or attraction for Kṛṣṇa; the seed-form of the permanent emotion; in bhāva-bhakti it first appears.
The peaceful devotional rasa, awareness of the Lord's greatness without personal intimacy (as of the sages); the first of the five primary rasas.
The rasa of servitude: love for Kṛṣṇa as master, with a sense of his superiority.
The rasa of friendship: love for Kṛṣṇa as an equal companion, as of the cowherd boys.
Parental love: love for Kṛṣṇa as one's child, as of Yaśodā and Nanda.
The amorous or 'brilliant' rasa, love for Kṛṣṇa as beloved, as of the gopīs; the highest of the five, treated in the Ujjvalanīlamaṇi.
The seven secondary rasas: humour, wonder, heroism, compassion, anger, fear and disgust, appearing within devotion.
Semblance of rasa: an improper or incompatible mixture of rasas, or rasa in an unfit object.
Devotion as practice, performed with the senses, whose aim is the manifestation of the eternally perfect bhāva in the heart.
Devotion by rule: practice impelled by the command of scripture, where spontaneous attraction (rāga) is not yet present.
Devotion consisting of rāga — spontaneous, intense absorption in the beloved — natural to the eternal residents of Vraja.
Devotion that follows the rāgātmikā devotion of the Vraja residents, arising from eager longing (lobha); of two kinds, kāmānugā and sambandhānugā.
Eager longing to attain the emotions of the Vraja residents — the sole qualification for rāgānugā practice.
The highest, pure devotion: favourable cultivation of Kṛṣṇa, free from other desires and uncovered by knowledge, works and the like.
Free from desires other than for Kṛṣṇa's service — the first mark of pure devotion.
Favourableness: devotion is cultivation of Kṛṣṇa in a way pleasing to him (not as enemies 'think' of him).
Devotion as emotion: the first sprouting of love, a ray of the sun of prema that softens the heart.
Emotion: the stage after attachment in Rūpa's sequence, pure sattva that softens the heart; in the Ujjvalanīlamaṇi also the name of mahābhāva's threshold.
Love for Kṛṣṇa: bhāva grown dense, melting the heart completely and marked by intense possessiveness toward him; the supreme goal, desiring only his pleasure (as opposed to kāma).
Faith — firm trust that by devotion to Kṛṣṇa all is accomplished; the first stage.
Association with saints — the second stage and one of the five most potent limbs.
Performance of devotional practice under a guru — the third stage.
Cessation of unwanted things (anartha) — the fourth stage.
Steadiness in practice, free from the obstacles of sleepiness, distraction and the like — the fifth stage.
Taste for practice itself — the sixth stage.
An unwanted thing obstructing devotion; of four kinds by origin (sin, pious acts, offences, devotion itself).
Love-pique: love so intense it takes the form of feigned anger or sulking, a stage above sneha.
Intimacy: love free of reverence, feeling oneness with the beloved.
Passion in which even sorrow becomes happiness for the beloved's sake.
Ever-new passion in which the beloved is experienced as ever fresh.
Great emotion, the summit of love, found only in the gopīs and fully in Rādhā; divided into rūḍha and adhirūḍha (with modana and mādana, the latter in Rādhā alone).
The mood of Rādhā's young maidservants (mañjarī), who serve the divine couple under Rādhā and seek no union with Kṛṣṇa for themselves; cultivated in rāgānugā practice through an inner identity.
The inner, perfected spiritual body/identity in which the practitioner serves in Vraja, alongside service in the practitioner's body (sādhaka-rūpa).

The transmission by the guru of the disciple's spiritual identity (name, form, age, dress, service, group, residence and the like) for meditation on the divine play; practised in the Nityānanda and Advaita lineages and among Vraja bābājīs, contested in the 20th c.
The eightfold daily play of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa from the end of night to night, the object of meditative remembrance (Govindalīlāmṛta, Kṛṣṇabhāvanāmṛta).
The semblance of the name: the name uttered without full attention or intent (e.g. by Ajāmila); destroys sin and gives liberation, but not love.
The 'great mantra' of sixteen names (hare kṛṣṇa … hare rāma …) from the Kalisantaraṇa Upaniṣad, chanted and sung without rules of time or place.
Congregational singing of the Lord's names, the dharma of the Kali age.
The instructing guru (may be many), as distinct from the one initiating guru (dīkṣā-guru).
The guru within the heart: the Lord as Paramātman guiding from within.
The triad structuring Gauḍīya theology: the relation (knowledge of Kṛṣṇa, souls and world), the means (devotion) and the goal (love).
Paramour love: love for Kṛṣṇa by those married to others, held by Rūpa (UN 1.21) to be the supreme form in Vraja; its status is the subject of the svakīyā–parakīyā debate.
Wedded love; Jīva holds the gopīs to be Kṛṣṇa's own (svakīyā) in truth, appearing as parakīyā in the manifest play.
Love in separation, which nourishes and intensifies union (sambhoga); in Caitanya's last years the dominant mood.
The Lord's own plenary expansions (Viṣṇu forms), non-different from him.
Separated parts: the souls, parts of his marginal power.
The fivefold truth: Caitanya, Nityānanda, Advaita, Gadādhara and Śrīvāsa as forms of Kṛṣṇa as devotee.
Fitting detachment: using things without attachment in Kṛṣṇa's service, as opposed to 'futile' renunciation (phalgu-vairāgya) of what relates to him.
Divine madness: the highest state of mahābhāva in separation, with speech such as citra-jalpa, seen in Rādhā and in Caitanya's last years.
Eternal servant: the soul's constitutional nature.
A spontaneous vivid manifestation of the Lord or his play in the devotee's heart, short of full direct vision.
The Lord's internal power that arranges his play, e.g. making the gopīs appear married to others and veiling his majesty.
Kṛṣṇa's highest abode, where he plays eternally with his associates; the manifest Vraja on earth is non-different from it.
The fifth human aim: love of Kṛṣṇa, beyond the four (dharma, artha, kāma, mokṣa).
Surrender, with six limbs: accepting the favourable, rejecting the unfavourable, faith in his protection, choosing him as protector, self-offering and humility.

equivalents.note: Gauḍīya and Nimbārka usage treat śaraṇāgati and prapatti as synonyms

definitions.definition: The Lord's name, non-different from him, a wish-fulfilling gem, fully empowered and manifesting itself on a tongue turned to service.
The names of Kṛṣṇa given at the first initiation (the refuge mantra) and sung in kīrtan.
An offence against the name; ten are listed (from the Padma Purāṇa), and they block the name's fruit of love.
Initiation, so called because it gives divine knowledge and destroys sin; the guru gives the mantras (gopāla-mantra, kāma-gāyatrī), which are not published.
Two initiations: the refuge mantra (nāma-nivedana) and the brahmasambandha.
Love in separation, which Vallabha holds to be the highest state of devotion (the gopīs' state).
Separation (vipralambha), exemplified in the Śikṣāṣṭaka 7 and in Caitanya's last years.
Denied by Bhāskara: while the body lasts, real adjuncts remain.
Redefined: one engaged in Hari's service in all conditions is jīvanmukta.
Oneness with Brahman after death, when the adjuncts fall away.
Attainment of the Lord's nature and non-separation from him, with difference preserved.
Held lower than loving service; puṣṭi devotees do not seek it.
Made to seem trivial by pure devotion; below prema, the fifth aim.
Equality with Śiva, free of bonds.
